hints: Think about whether forming bonds between gaseous ions, or forming bonds between ions and water, releases energy or absorbs energy.
walkthrough:
Remember what releases energy**
Forming attractions always releases energy, so it is exothermic. When gaseous $\text{Ca}^{2+}$ and $\text{Br}^{-}$ come together to make a solid lattice, strong ionic bonds form. When gaseous ions are surrounded by water molecules, ion-dipole bonds form. Both processes give out heat, so $\Delta H_{latt}^{\ominus}$ and $\Delta H_{hyd}^{\ominus}$ are always negative.

See solution as a balance of two steps**
Dissolving is a tug of war. You first break the lattice apart, which takes in energy ($-\Delta H_{latt}^{\ominus}$, endothermic), then you hydrate the ions, which gives out energy (exothermic). Sometimes hydration wins and the overall $\Delta H_{sol}^{\ominus}$ is negative, sometimes the lattice cost wins and it is positive. So solution can be either sign.
Final answer: lattice energy: always negative; enthalpy change of hydration: always negative; enthalpy change of solution: can be either negative or positive.

hints: Focus on the start and end states: where do the ions start (gas or solid) and where do they end up, and for how many moles?
walkthrough:
Build the definition piece by piece**
Picture one mole of isolated ions floating in the gas phase, for example $\text{Ca}^{2+}(\text{g})$. Now drop them into a large amount of water so each ion becomes surrounded by water molecules: $\text{Ca}^{2+}(\text{aq})$. The heat change for that exact change, $\text{X}^{+/-}(\text{g}) \rightarrow \text{X}^{+/-}(\text{aq})$, is the enthalpy change of hydration. Remember to state 1 mole and gaseous to aqueous.
Final answer: The enthalpy change when 1 mole of gaseous ions is dissolved in water to form aqueous ions.

hints: Sketch the Born-Haber route from elements to solid $\text{CaBr}_{2}(\text{s})$ via gaseous atoms and then gaseous ions, and place $\Delta H_{f}^{\ominus}$ on the direct arrow.
List which Table 8.2 values make the gaseous ions: atomisation of Ca, first and second ionisation of Ca, atomisation of Br, and electron affinity of Br, remembering the formula has two bromides.
Write the Hess cycle equation $\Delta H_{f} = \Delta H_{at}(\text{Ca}) + IE_{1} + IE_{2} + 2\Delta H_{at}(\text{Br}) + 2EA_{1} + \Delta H_{latt}$ and rearrange for $\Delta H_{latt}$.
walkthrough:
Set up the Born-Haber picture**
Imagine two ways to make $\text{CaBr}_{2}(\text{s})$ from $\text{Ca}(\text{s}) + \text{Br}_{2}(\text{l})$. The short direct way is $\Delta H_{f}^{\ominus} = -682.8 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$. The long way goes up to gaseous atoms and ions then down into the lattice: $$\text{Ca}(\text{s}) \rightarrow \text{Ca}(\text{g}) \rightarrow \text{Ca}^{2+}(\text{g})$$ $$2\text{Br} \rightarrow 2\text{Br}(\text{g}) \rightarrow 2\text{Br}^{-}(\text{g}) \rightarrow \text{CaBr}_{2}(\text{s})$$ By Hess law both routes have the same total energy change.

Pick only the six needed numbers**
From Table 8.2 you need: $\Delta H_{at}(\text{Ca}) = +178.2$, $IE_{1} = +590$, $IE_{2} = +1145$, $\Delta H_{at}(\text{Br}) = +111.9$, $EA_{1}(\text{Br}) = -324.6$, and $\Delta H_{f} = -682.8$, all in $\text{kJ mol}^{-1}$. Ignore $\text{Br-Br}$ bond energy, $\Delta H_{sol}$, $\Delta H_{hyd}$ and ionisation of bromine. They belong to different cycles. Because the formula is $\text{CaBr}_{2}$, you need two Br atoms and two electron affinities.

Substitute and solve for lattice energy**
Write the Hess sum: $$\Delta H_{f}^{\ominus} = 178.2 + 590 + 1145 + 2(111.9) + 2(-324.6) + \Delta H_{latt}^{\ominus}$$ Add the bracket: $178.2 + 590 + 1145 = 1913.2$, $2(111.9) = 223.8$, $2(-324.6) = -649.2$. Total upward cost $= 1913.2 + 223.8 - 649.2 = +1487.8 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$. Rearrange: $$\Delta H_{latt}^{\ominus} = -682.8 - 1487.8 = -2170.6 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$$ The large negative sign makes sense because bringing $\text{Ca}^{2+}$ and $2\text{Br}^{-}$ together releases a lot of energy.

Final answer: $\Delta H_{latt}^{\ominus} = \Delta H_{f}^{\ominus} - [\Delta H_{at}(\text{Ca}) + IE_{1} + IE_{2} + 2\Delta H_{at}(\text{Br}) + 2EA_{1}]$
$= -682.8 - [178.2 + 590 + 1145 + 2(111.9) + 2(-324.6)] = -2170.6 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$

hints: Draw the solution cycle with solid $\text{CaBr}_{2}$ going to gaseous ions (reverse of lattice formation) then to aqueous ions via hydration.
Write the Hess expression $\Delta H_{sol} = -\Delta H_{latt} + \Delta H_{hyd}(\text{Ca}^{2+}) + 2\Delta H_{hyd}(\text{Br}^{-})$ and identify the three known values.
walkthrough:
See dissolving in two stages**
Start with $\text{CaBr}_{2}(\text{s})$. First break it into $\text{Ca}^{2+}(\text{g}) + 2\text{Br}^{-}(\text{g})$. That is the opposite of lattice formation, so its energy is $-\Delta H_{latt}^{\ominus} = -(-2170.6) = +2170.6 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$. Then hydrate each gaseous ion: $\text{Ca}^{2+}(\text{g}) \rightarrow \text{Ca}^{2+}(\text{aq})$ gives $-1579 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$, and each $\text{Br}^{-}$ gives an unknown $x$.

Solve with Hess law**
The sum must equal the measured $\Delta H_{sol}^{\ominus} = -103.1 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$: $$-103.1 = 2170.6 - 1579 + 2x$$ Combine: $2170.6 - 1579 = 591.6$. So $2x = -103.1 - 591.6 = -694.7$. Therefore: $$x = \frac{-694.7}{2} = -347.35 \approx -347 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$$ That is $\Delta H_{hyd}^{\ominus}$ of $\text{Br}^{-}$. Do not forget the factor of 2, a very common slip.

Final answer: $\Delta H_{sol}^{\ominus} = -\Delta H_{latt}^{\ominus} + \Delta H_{hyd}^{\ominus}(\text{Ca}^{2+}) + 2\Delta H_{hyd}^{\ominus}(\text{Br}^{-})$
$-103.1 = +2170.6 - 1579 + 2\Delta H_{hyd}^{\ominus}(\text{Br}^{-})$
$\Delta H_{hyd}^{\ominus}(\text{Br}^{-}) = -347 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$ (approx $-347.4$).

hints: Compare the sizes of $\text{Br}^{-}$ and $\text{I}^{-}$ using their positions in Group 17 and number of electron shells.
Think about how ionic size controls how closely water dipoles can approach the ion centre and how strong the attraction will be.
walkthrough:
Compare the ionic sizes**
Both ions carry the same $1-$ charge, but bromide is above iodide in Group 17. $\text{Br}^{-}$ has electrons in $n=4$ as its outer shell while $\text{I}^{-}$ extends to $n=5$, so $\text{Br}^{-}$ is distinctly smaller. Same charge packed into a smaller volume means higher charge density.

Link size to attraction to water**
Hydration energy comes from ion-dipole bonds between the anion and the $\delta+$ hydrogen atoms of water. A smaller $\text{Br}^{-}$ lets water molecules get closer to the centre of charge, so electrostatic attraction $\propto q/r$ is stronger. Stronger bonds formed means more energy is released, so $\Delta H_{hyd}^{\ominus}$ is more negative (more exothermic) for $\text{Br}^{-}$ than for $\text{I}^{-}$.

Final answer: $\text{Br}^{-}$ has a smaller ionic radius than $\text{I}^{-}$ (fewer shells).
Therefore $\text{Br}^{-}$ has a higher charge density and forms stronger ion-dipole attractions with water molecules, releasing more energy on hydration.
